notes.meaning: The Lord gives Moses new instructions for when someone sins by accident or human weakness against any of His commandments. A sin offering is required because even mistakes and unintentional wrongs still violate God's law. In God's eyes, not knowing or not thinking does not take away the guilt of doing what He forbade.

differ.view: Reformed teachers emphasize that unintentional sins include human weakness where a believer stumbles and repents, in contrast to defiant sins done with a rebellious heart.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate this term as a purification offering, arguing that its main purpose was to cleanse God's sanctuary from the pollution of sin.

notes.meaning: The instructions begin with the anointed high priest, who was set apart with holy oil to lead the people before God. If he falls into sin, his position makes the guilt heavier because his bad example can lead the whole nation into error. For this reason, he must bring a young bull without any defects, which was the largest and most valuable animal sacrifice.

The high priest brings the bull to the entrance of the sacred tent and places his hand firmly on the animal's head. By this action, he confesses his sin and transfers his guilt to the innocent animal that will die in his place. Then the bull is slaughtered before the Lord, showing that sin deserves death.

differ.view: Baptists emphasize that pressing down hard on the animal's head pictures the heavy, personal resting of faith completely upon Christ as substitute.

notes.meaning: The priest collects some of the bull's blood and carries it inside the Tent of Meeting. Sacrificial blood was usually handled in the outer courtyard, so bringing it into the holy tent showed how serious the high priest's sin was. The blood had to be brought closer to God's presence to seek reconciliation.

The priest dips his finger into the blood and sprinkles it seven times before the Lord in front of the inner sanctuary curtain. In the Bible, the number seven points to completeness and perfection. This repeated sprinkling showed the complete work needed to restore the covenant relationship that sin had damaged.

The priest smears some blood onto the four horns of the golden altar where fragrant incense was burned in God's presence. Then he pours the rest of the blood out at the base of the bronze altar in the outer courtyard. Putting blood on the incense altar showed that the priest's sin had hurt his prayers and ministry, which now had to be purified.

The priest removes all the inner fat from the bull, along with the two kidneys and the lobe of the liver. He burns these choice portions on the altar of burnt offering, just as was done with the peace offerings. Giving the richest inner parts to God honored Him and showed that the best was devoted to His glory.

The priests are not allowed to eat any part of this bull, so the entire body, hide, and waste are carried outside the camp. The carcass is completely burned on a wood fire in a ceremonially clean ash heap. This burning outside the camp showed how hateful sin is to God, and it pointed forward to Jesus suffering outside the city gates for us.

If the entire community breaks one of God's commands without realizing it, the people still carry guilt before the Lord. An entire nation can be led astray by bad customs or mistaken leaders. As soon as the sin is recognized, the whole congregation must bring a young bull as a sin offering to the entrance of the tent.

The elders of the congregation lay their hands on the head of the bull before the Lord. Because the whole crowd cannot physically touch the sacrifice, the elders act as their representatives to confess the nation's guilt. The animal is then slaughtered before the Lord to bear the penalty for the people.

The anointed priest brings the blood inside the Tent of Meeting, just as he did for his own sin offering. He sprinkles it seven times before the veil and puts blood on the horns of the incense altar. Then he pours the rest at the base of the outer altar, purifying the sanctuary from the nation's sin.

The priest burns all the fat on the altar and takes the rest of the bull outside the camp to be destroyed by fire. Through this ritual, the priest makes atonement, which means removing guilt and restoring peace with God, and the congregation is forgiven. This complete removal of the animal pictured the total putting away of the people's sin.

When a ruler or political leader sins unintentionally against any commandment, he becomes guilty. Even though a ruler has authority over others, he is still directly accountable to the Lord his God. High rank does not place any leader above God's law.

When the ruler realizes his mistake, he must bring a male goat without any blemish as his offering. He lays his hand on the goat's head and slaughters it in the courtyard where burnt offerings are killed. A male goat was required for a ruler, showing that his public office made his sin more serious than that of an ordinary person.

The priest puts some of the goat's blood on the horns of the courtyard altar and pours the rest at its base. Then he burns all its fat on the altar, making atonement for the ruler so that he is forgiven. Unlike the offering for a high priest, this blood was not taken inside the tent, showing a lesser degree of ceremonial contamination.

When an everyday person sins unintentionally against any of God's commandments, that individual is still guilty. Once the person becomes aware of the sin, the required offering is an unblemished female goat. God watches over common people just as He does kings, and none of them are forgotten or left without a way to be restored.

The worshiper lays a hand on the goat's head, slaughters it, and the priest applies the blood to the horns of the courtyard altar. The fat is burned on the fire as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, and the priest makes atonement so the person is forgiven. Even the humblest offering, brought in honest repentance, is fully acceptable to God.

If a common person brings a sheep instead of a goat, the offering must be an unblemished female lamb. The person places a hand on its head and slaughters it where burnt offerings are killed. God provides this option to accommodate the worshiper while still requiring a perfect, innocent substitute.

The priest puts the lamb's blood on the horns of the altar, pours out the rest at the bottom, and burns its fat with the fire offerings. Through this act, atonement is made for the sin that was committed, and the person receives forgiveness. These Old Testament sacrifices pointed forward to Jesus Christ, the true Lamb who takes away all sin.
